steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our adversarial robustness paper that presents LAST ("Learn from the Past"), a defense framework that uses the model's historical parameter states as a proxy model plus a self-distillation regularizer. Cover the background on adversarial attacks and adversarial training, the limits of current methods, our idea and framework, the loss-landscape visualization, the contributions, and how the paper is organized.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Adversarial vulnerability
  - deep models widely deployed in real-world applications (cite)
  - susceptible to subtle adversarial perturbations in input (cite)
  - perturbed samples -> specified or other wrong predictions; threatens real-world surveillance (cite), autonomous driving (cite); safety concerns
  - so robustness against adversarial samples from various attacks = focal research topic (cite)
- Adversarial training
  - diverse defenses explored (cite); Adversarial Training (AT) (cite) among most effective; essence: min-max optimization
  - following iterative attacks (cite), Standard AT (SAT) = single-step (cite) and multi-step (cite) paradigms
  - single-step, e.g. Fast-AT (cite): computational efficiency, fast convergence
  - multi-step, e.g. PGD-AT (cite): robustness with larger datasets, more training cost
  - heuristic enhancements (cite): special regularization terms (cite), extra robust teacher models (cite)
  - YOPO: Pontryagin's Maximum Principle (PMP) to decouple adversary update and back-propagation
  - Fast-AT-GA (cite): regularizer maximizing gradient alignment in perturbation set; improves Fast-AT robustness, narrows gap to complex AT
  - Fast-BAT (cite): bi-level optimization + implicit gradients
  - KD-AT: mitigates label noise by recalibrating adversarial example labels with predictive distribution of adversarially trained model
- Limitations
  - these methods add prior knowledge or new learning strategies to help the current target model, at explicit or implicit cost
  - SAT-based methods: unstable convergence of target model (cite)
  - catastrophic overfitting (cite): big performance drop during training, limits robustness
  - perturbations from SAT inner maximization use gradients of target model's current parameters -> stronger attack
- Our idea and framework
  - historical parameter states + gradient directions are hidden from adversarial examples -> defense prior
  - LAST (Learn from the Past): historical states as proxy model
  - proxy response -> dynamically learned fast weights -> differential unit = corrected gradient direction for target update
  - self-distillation regularized objective: guides proxy update trajectory, no extra teacher, alleviates catastrophic overfitting
  - experiments: CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImagenet; PreActResNet-18, WideResNet-34-10
  - consistent, significant gains in training stability and final robustness; for single-step and multi-step AT
- Visualization of adversarial landscapes
  - Fig. 1: adversarial loss landscape (cite) w.r.t. input variations; Fast-AT, Fast-AT-FA, Fast-BAT, PGD-AT vs LAST versions; PreActResNet-18, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}=8/255, CIFAR10
  - loss computed along sign gradient direction and random (Rademacher) direction from the clean image; loss gaps between max and min loss for x,y\in[-0.25,0.25]
  - stronger defense -> less sensitive, lower loss, smoother landscape, smaller gap
  - LAST: lower loss, smoother surfaces, smaller gaps -> more robust to adversarial and random perturbations
- Contributions
  - new perspective: use historical states' response, better initial values + defensive prior
  - general framework LAST: historical states as proxy, fast weights adjust target update direction; improves single- and multi-step AT; alternative to SAT pipeline
  - self-distillation defense objective, no external teacher, mitigates catastrophic overfitting
  - extensive evaluation: up to \bf 9.2\% and \bf 20.3\% RA increase vs PGD-AT under AutoAttack (\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=16/255) on CIFAR10/CIFAR100; better stability, less overfitting
- Organization: Sec. II related work (attacks, defenses, historical states); Sec. III AT fundamentals, motivation, LAST, theory; Sec. IV implementation, results, ablation; Sect. V conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning models are now widely deployed in real-world applications, and people increasingly recognize that these models are susceptible to subtle adversarial perturbations in the input data. When perturbed adversarial samples are introduced, the target model can produce specified or other wrong predictions, which can put at risk the functionality of real-world surveillance and autonomous driving systems, and this raises critical safety concerns. Because of this, improving model robustness against adversarial samples generated by various attacks has become a focal research topic.

Many different defense techniques have been explored to mitigate adversarial attacks, but Adversarial Training (AT) is widely seen as one of the most effective strategies, and its essence is solving the min-max optimization problem. Following the iterative format of adversarial attacks, Standard AT (SAT) methods mainly include single-step and multi-step training paradigms. Roughly, single-step AT (e.g., Fast-AT) focuses on computational efficiency so the solution converges fast, while multi-step AT (e.g., PGD-AT) mainly aims to increase robustness with larger datasets and more training cost. On top of that, several lines of work have explored heuristic defense techniques to enhance the defense process, e.g., adding special regularization terms or additional robust teacher models. YOPO uses the Pontryagin's Maximum Principle (PMP) to decouple the adversary update and back-propagation processes in AT. Fast-AT-GA introduces a new regularization term that maximizes gradient alignment within the perturbation set, which improves Fast-AT's robustness and reduces the performance gap with more complex adversarial training methods. Fast-BAT refines AT with a bi-level optimization strategy and implicit gradient computation to make training more robust. KD-AT proposes to mitigate label noise by recalibrating the labels of adversarial examples, using the predictive label distribution of an adversarially trained model.

In short, these methods basically put effort into introducing extra prior knowledge or designing new learning strategies to help the current state of the target model defend against adversarial examples, with explicit or implicit cost. However, existing methods based on SAT always suffer from unstable convergence of the target model. Also, the catastrophic overfitting problem limits how much robustness can improve; it means a big performance decrease during the training process. The adversarial perturbations are crafted in the attack's inner maximization loop of SAT using the gradients of the target model's current parameters, and this makes them better at jeopardizing the target model.

- Our idea and framework
  - historical parameter states + gradient directions hidden from adversarial examples -> defense prior
  - LAST (Learn from the Past): historical states as proxy model; fast weights -> differential unit -> corrected update direction
  - self-distillation regularized objective, no extra teacher, alleviates catastrophic overfitting
  - CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImagenet; PreActResNet-18, WideResNet-34-10; better stability + robustness for single- and multi-step AT
- Visualization of adversarial landscapes (Fig. 1)
  - Fast-AT, Fast-AT-FA, Fast-BAT, PGD-AT vs LAST versions; PreActResNet-18, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}=8/255, CIFAR10
  - loss along sign gradient + Rademacher random direction; loss gaps for x,y\in[-0.25,0.25]
  - LAST: lower loss, smoother surfaces, smaller gaps
- Contributions: new perspective; general framework LAST; self-distillation defense; extensive evaluation (up to \bf 9.2\% and \bf 20.3\% RA gain vs PGD-AT under AutoAttack (\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=16/255))
- Organization: Sec. II related work; Sec. III method + theory; Sec. IV experiments + ablation; Sect. V conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning models are now widely deployed in real-world applications, and people increasingly recognize that these models are susceptible to subtle adversarial perturbations in the input data. When perturbed adversarial samples are introduced, the target model can produce specified or other wrong predictions, which can put at risk the functionality of real-world surveillance and autonomous driving systems, and this raises critical safety concerns. Because of this, improving model robustness against adversarial samples generated by various attacks has become a focal research topic.

Many different defense techniques have been explored to mitigate adversarial attacks, but Adversarial Training (AT) is widely seen as one of the most effective strategies, and its essence is solving the min-max optimization problem. Following the iterative format of adversarial attacks, Standard AT (SAT) methods mainly include single-step and multi-step training paradigms. Roughly, single-step AT (e.g., Fast-AT) focuses on computational efficiency so the solution converges fast, while multi-step AT (e.g., PGD-AT) mainly aims to increase robustness with larger datasets and more training cost. On top of that, several lines of work have explored heuristic defense techniques to enhance the defense process, e.g., adding special regularization terms or additional robust teacher models. YOPO uses the Pontryagin's Maximum Principle (PMP) to decouple the adversary update and back-propagation processes in AT. Fast-AT-GA introduces a new regularization term that maximizes gradient alignment within the perturbation set, which improves Fast-AT's robustness and reduces the performance gap with more complex adversarial training methods. Fast-BAT refines AT with a bi-level optimization strategy and implicit gradient computation to make training more robust. KD-AT proposes to mitigate label noise by recalibrating the labels of adversarial examples, using the predictive label distribution of an adversarially trained model.

In short, these methods basically put effort into introducing extra prior knowledge or designing new learning strategies to help the current state of the target model defend against adversarial examples, with explicit or implicit cost. However, existing methods based on SAT always suffer from unstable convergence of the target model. Also, the catastrophic overfitting problem limits how much robustness can improve; it means a big performance decrease during the training process. The adversarial perturbations are crafted in the attack's inner maximization loop of SAT using the gradients of the target model's current parameters, and this makes them better at jeopardizing the target model.

In this work, we point out that during defense, the historical parameter states of the target model and their gradient directions stay hidden, so they are unknown to the adversarial examples and can provide a defense prior. From this new perspective, we build a universal adversarial defense framework called 'LAST' (Learn from the Past), which uses the model's historical states as the proxy model to strengthen defense. Specifically, we first generate a response based on the proxy model to get dynamically learned fast weights, which are used to calculate the differential unit as the corrected gradient direction for the target model's next update. We also propose a self-distillation regularized defense objective that guides the update trajectory of the proxy model without needing extra teacher models and effectively reduces the effect of catastrophic overfitting on performance. In experiments on datasets of different scales (CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and TinyImagenet) and with different network architectures (PreActResNet-18 and WideResNet-34-10), we do comprehensive evaluations showing that LAST brings consistent and significant improvements to both training stability and final robustness. These improvements show up for both single-step and multi-step AT based on the SAT formulation.

Visualization of Adversarial Landscapes. In Fig. 1, we compare the adversarial loss landscape w.r.t. input variations for four SAT methods, Fast-AT, Fast-AT-FA, Fast-BAT and PGD-AT, and their improved versions under the LAST framework, trained with the PreActResNet-18 backbone with \boldsymbol{\epsilon}=8/255 on the CIFAR10 dataset. The adversarial loss is calculated with \mathcal{L}_{\mathtt{atk}}(\boldsymbol{u}+x\boldsymbol{\vec{\iota}}+y\boldsymbol{\vec{o}}), where \boldsymbol{u} is the clean image, and \boldsymbol{\vec{\iota}}=\mathtt{sgn}(\nabla_{\mathbf{I}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathtt{atk}}(\boldsymbol{u}) and \boldsymbol{\vec{o}}\sim\textrm{Rademacher}(0,0.5) are the sign gradient direction and the random direction used to add the perturbation (x and y are the linear coefficients). We also calculate the loss gaps between the max and min losses in the range x,y\in[-0.25,0.25]. Generally, models with stronger defense are less sensitive to adversarial examples made by adding mixed perturbation along the gradient direction and the random direction, so they have lower overall loss, smoother loss landscapes and a smaller loss gap. We can see that the loss landscapes of models trained with LAST have lower loss, smoother surfaces and smaller loss gaps, so they are more robust against both adversarial and random perturbations of different scales. Our main contributions are summarized below.

- 1. New perspective. Unlike existing approaches that only rely on the target model for adversarial defense, this study is the first to integrate the response of historical states, which uses the better initial values and defensive prior to defend.

- 2. General Defense Framework. We develop a universal adversarial defense framework, LAST, which uses the historical states of the target model as a proxy model and keeps adjusting the update direction of the target model with dynamically learned fast weights. The framework consistently improves existing single-step and multi-step AT methods and is an alternative to the commonly used SAT pipeline.

- 3. Self Distillation Defense. Using the proxy model, we also design a self-distillation regularized defense objective that constrains the update direction of the proxy model without external teacher models, which effectively reduces the impact of catastrophic overfitting.

- 4. Extensive Evaluation. We implement LAST on top of various SAT methods and verify that it consistently improves performance (e.g., up to \bf 9.2\% and \bf 20.3\% increase of RA compared with PGD-AT under AutoAttack (\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=16/255) on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets, respectively) with different backbones, datasets and attack modalities, and we also show it can improve training stability and reduce overfitting issues.

The rest of this work is organized as follows. Sec. II is about adversarial attacks and defenses and reviews related work that uses the historical states of parameters. In Sec. III, we introduce the fundamentals of adversarial training, the motivation for using historical states, how the LAST defense framework is built, and give theoretical analyses and discussions. Sec. IV describes implementation details like experimental parameters, quantifies and visualizes the results, and discusses the ablation study. Sect. V concludes this work.

steps.text:
In the context of deep learning models and their widespread deployment in real-world applications [1,2,3], there is growing recognition of the susceptibility of these models to subtle adversarial perturbations in input data [4,5,6]. Introducing perturbed adversarial samples can lead the target model to produce specified or alternative erroneous predictions, jeopardizing the functionality of real-world surveillance [7] and autonomous driving systems [8], and giving rise to critical safety concerns. Consequently, enhancing model robustness against adversarial samples generated by various attacks has emerged as a focal research topic [9,10,11].

While diversified defense techniques [12,13] have been explored to mitigate adversarial attacks, Adversarial Training (AT) [14,15] is widely acknowledged as among the most effective strategies, and its essence lies in solving the min-max optimization problem. In line with the iterative format of adversarial attacks [16,17], Standard AT (SAT) methods mainly encompass single-step [18] and multi-step [14] training paradigms. Broadly speaking, single-step AT (e.g., Fast-AT [19]) prioritizes computational efficiency to allow rapid convergence, whereas multi-step AT (e.g., PGD-AT [20]) is mainly dedicated to improving robustness with larger datasets and increased training cost. On top of that, several lines of work have explored heuristic defense techniques to enhance the defense process [21,22], e.g., introducing specialized regularization terms [12] or additional robust teacher models [20,23]. YOPO employs the Pontryagin's Maximum Principle (PMP) to decouple the adversary update and back-propagation processes in AT. Fast-AT-GA [24] introduces a new regularization term that maximizes gradient alignment within the perturbation set, improving Fast-AT's robustness and reducing the performance gap with more complex adversarial training methods. Fast-BAT [25] refines AT by employing a bi-level optimization strategy and implicit gradient computation to make training more robust. KD-AT proposes mitigating label noise by recalibrating the labels assigned to adversarial examples, using the predictive label distribution of an adversarially trained model.

To summarize, these methods essentially spend effort on introducing additional prior knowledge or designing new learning strategies to help the current state of the target model defend against adversarial examples, at explicit or implicit cost. However, existing SAT-based methods always suffer from unstable convergence of the target model [23,26]. Meanwhile, the catastrophic overfitting [27] problem, which refers to a significant performance decrease during training, also limits robustness improvement. The adversarial perturbations crafted within the attack's inner maximization loop of SAT leverage the gradient information of the target model's current parameters, which enhances their capacity to jeopardize the target model.

In this work, we emphasize that during the defense process, the historical parameter states of the target model and their corresponding gradient directions remain concealed, so they are unknown to the adversarial examples and provide a defense prior. From this new perspective, we establish a universal adversarial defense framework named 'LAST' (Learn from the Past), which incorporates the model's historical states as the proxy model to fortify defense. Specifically, we first generate a response based on the proxy model to derive dynamically learned fast weights, which are used to calculate the differential unit as the corrected gradient direction for the target model's subsequent update. Besides, we propose a self-distillation regularized defense objective that directs the update trajectory of the proxy model without additional teacher models and effectively alleviates the impact of catastrophic overfitting on performance. Experimentally, across datasets of varying scales (i.e., CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImagenet) and with diverse network architectures (i.e., PreActResNet-18 and WideResNet-34-10), we conduct comprehensive evaluations that substantiate the consistent and significant enhancement LAST brings to both training stability and final robustness. These enhancements are evidenced through improvements in single-step and multi-step AT based on the SAT formulation.

Visualization of Adversarial Landscapes. In Fig. 1, we compare the adversarial loss landscape [28] w.r.t. input variations between four SAT methods, Fast-AT, Fast-AT-FA, Fast-BAT and PGD-AT, and their improved versions under the LAST framework, trained using the PreActResNet-18 backbone with \boldsymbol{\epsilon}=8/255 on the CIFAR10 dataset. The adversarial loss is calculated with \mathcal{L}_{\mathtt{atk}}(\boldsymbol{u}+x\boldsymbol{\vec{\iota}}+y\boldsymbol{\vec{o}}), where \boldsymbol{u} denotes the clean image, and \boldsymbol{\vec{\iota}}=\mathtt{sgn}(\nabla_{\mathbf{I}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathtt{atk}}(\boldsymbol{u}) and \boldsymbol{\vec{o}}\sim\textrm{Rademacher}(0,0.5) are the sign gradient direction and random direction used to introduce the perturbation (x and y are the corresponding linear coefficients). We also calculate the loss gaps between the maximum and minimum losses within the range x,y\in[-0.25,0.25]. Typically, models with stronger defense capabilities are less sensitive to adversarial examples generated by adding mixed perturbation along the gradient direction and random direction, and thus exhibit lower overall loss, smoother loss landscapes and a smaller loss gap. As can be observed, the loss landscapes of models trained with the LAST framework show lower loss, smoother surfaces and smaller loss gaps, exhibiting enhanced robustness against both adversarial and random perturbations of different scales. We summarize our main contributions as follows.

- 1. New perspective. Diverging from existing approaches that depend solely on the target model for adversarial defense, this study pioneers the integration of the historical states' response, which leverages enhanced initial values and a defensive prior to defend.

- 2. General Defense Framework. We develop a universal adversarial defense framework, LAST, which incorporates the historical states of the target model as a proxy model and continuously adjusts the update direction of the target model with dynamically learned fast weights. This framework consistently improves existing single-step and multi-step AT methods, offering an alternative to the commonly used SAT pipeline.

- 3. Self Distillation Defense. Leveraging the introduced proxy model, we further design a self-distillation regularized defense objective that constrains the update direction of the proxy model without external teacher models, effectively mitigating the impact of catastrophic overfitting.

- 4. Extensive Evaluation. We implement the LAST framework on various SAT methods and verify its consistent performance improvement (e.g., up to \bf 9.2\% and \bf 20.3\% increase of RA compared with PGD-AT under AutoAttack (\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=16/255) on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets, respectively) across different backbones, datasets and attack modalities, and also demonstrate its ability to enhance training stability and ameliorate overfitting issues.

The rest of this work is organized as follows. Sec. II discusses adversarial attacks and defenses and reviews related work that leverages the historical states of parameters. In Sec. III, we introduce the fundamentals of adversarial training, the motivation for referencing historical states, and the construction of the LAST defense framework, and provide relevant theoretical analyses and discussions. Sec. IV describes implementation details such as experimental parameters, quantifies and visualizes the experimental results, and discusses the ablation study. Sect. V concludes this work.
